claim: Only the 'pure discounting' component of real interest-rate changes transmits one-for-one to equity valuations; growth-driven and risk-driven rate changes transmit weakly or negatively.
stance_target: the naive assumption that equity discount rates move one-for-one with any observed interest-rate change
quoted_support: Only pure-discounting shocks should transmit one-for-one to valuations, with weak-to-negative transmission from growth and risk.

claim: Pure-discounting shocks explain 80% of cross-country equity valuation changes since 1990, while the raw (undecomposed) change in trend real rates is essentially uncorrelated with the change in equity yield across G7 countries (adjusted R-squared of -0.02).
stance_target: the query's premise that discount-rate changes compress valuations, but ONLY the pure-discounting subcomponent, not rate changes generally
scope_conditions: G7 economies, 1990-2023, using survey growth forecasts and asset prices
quoted_support: pure-discounting shocks indeed transmit one-for-one to equity and explain 80% of cross-country valuation changes since 1990.

claim: Only 35% of the post-1990 decline in U.S. real interest rates is attributable to pure discounting; the remainder reflects changes in expected growth or risk, which do not mechanically re-rate equities.
stance_target: the assumption that the full observed decline in US rates should be capitalized into equity multiples
quoted_support: In the U.S., we find that 35% of the interest-rate decline is attributable to pure discounting, implying that only a fraction of the change in rates has passed through directly to equities.

claim: Sorting US stocks into five duration quintiles by IBES analyst long-term-growth forecasts, regressions of 3-year returns on 3-year changes in the pure-discounting term give a slope of about -10 for the shortest-cash-flow-duration quintile and about -30 for the longest-duration quintile, implying the longest-duration portfolio has roughly 3x the cash-flow duration of the shortest, with a lower-bound duration gap of about 20 years.
stance_target: long-duration equities are measurably more exposed to (pure-discounting) rate shocks than short-duration equities
scope_conditions: US stocks, 1990-2023, duration proxied by analyst long-term growth forecast quintile
quoted_support: the portfolio of firms with the shortest cash-flow duration has a slope coefficient of around -10, while the portfolio of firms with the longest cash-flow duration has a slope of -30... the portfolio of firms with the longest duration has three times as long a cash-flow duration as the portfolio of firms with the shortest duration. A lower bound on this difference appears to be 20 years.

claim: When the same duration-sorted portfolios are regressed on the RAW nominal 10-year Treasury yield change (rather than the isolated pure-discounting term), all quintiles show small, statistically weak, and sometimes wrong-signed loadings -- equity duration does not predict sensitivity to an arbitrary/raw interest-rate change, only to the pure-discounting subcomponent specifically.
stance_target: the general claim that 'long-duration equities are more sensitive to interest-rate changes' when 'interest rate change' means any observed rate move rather than the isolated pure-discounting shock
quoted_support: equity duration does not correspond to the price sensitivity of equity to an arbitrary change in interest rates. Instead, only pure discounting shocks induce interest-rate variation that passes through to equity in proportion to its duration.

claim: A naive calculation assuming a 30-year duration gap between growth and value stocks and the full ~3pp US rate decline being pure discounting would imply ~90 percentage points of relative growth-stock outperformance (over 4%/year over 20 years), enough to erase the historical value premium -- but because only ~1pp of the ~3pp decline is pure discounting and the actual duration spread is well under 30 years, the real contribution to value's underperformance is much smaller than this naive estimate.
stance_target: naive point estimates of rate-driven equity re-rating that ignore the growth/risk/pure-discounting decomposition
quoted_support: while interest rates have dropped by close to 3 percentage points in the U.S., the pure discounting term has dropped by only about 1 percentage point, and it is only this component that should pass through to long-duration assets... The net effect on the realized return on the value factor is therefore substantially smaller.

claim: Comparing realized stock returns to duration-matched Treasury bond returns (as in van Binsbergen and Polk-Vuolteenaho) shows near-zero excess stock returns in recent decades, but this is only a valid benchmark for the pure-discounting subcomponent of rates -- unadjusted bond returns are not generally a good benchmark for equities because most of the rate decline reflects growth/risk shocks with different equity pass-through.
stance_target: whether duration-matched bond comparisons validly measure the realized equity risk premium
quoted_support: Our analysis lends support to one aspect of these papers' argument, as we show in Result 3 that a duration-matched rate measure is indeed the relevant benchmark for equity. That result, however, applies to one specific rate measure: the pure discount rate. Unadjusted bond returns, by contrast, may not be a good benchmark for stocks.
